summary: This unit covers the inborn immune defects: X-linked agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, DiGeorge syndrome, and SCID. The exam gives you an infection pattern and an age of onset, and asks you to name the broken arm of the immune system, the gene, and the first test to order.

points: B cell or antibody defect: encapsulated bacteria (S pneumoniae, H influenzae), enteroviruses, Giardia; sinus and lung infections.
T cell defect: viruses, fungi (Candida), Pneumocystis, intracellular organisms; failure to thrive.
Combined T and B defect (SCID): bacteria, viruses, fungi, and Pneumocystis, starting in the first months of life.
Phagocyte defect (chronic granulomatous disease): catalase-positive organisms such as S aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia.
Terminal complement (C5 to C9) defect: recurrent Neisseria infections.
Antibody defects show up after about 6 months, when maternal IgG fades.
notes.why: Each arm of immunity handles a different kind of pathogen, so the infection list points to the broken arm. Opsonizing antibody with complement clears encapsulated bacteria, and neutralizing and mucosal antibody controls enteroviruses and Giardia, while T cells and Th1-activated macrophages handle viruses, fungi, and intracellular organisms. Neutrophil NADPH oxidase is needed to kill catalase-positive organisms, and the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9) is uniquely important for lysing Neisseria. Antibody defects stay hidden early because maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the infant for the first months.

points: Mutation in BTK (Bruton tyrosine kinase) on the X chromosome; almost always boys.
Pre-B cells cannot mature into B cells, so blood B cells (CD19 or CD20) are absent.
All immunoglobulin classes are very low.
Tonsils and lymph nodes are small because they lack germinal centers.
Infections: encapsulated bacteria, enteroviral meningoencephalitis, vaccine polio, Giardia.
Avoid live vaccines.
notes.why: BTK carries the signal from the pre-B cell receptor, so without it B cell development stops at the pre-B stage in the marrow. No mature B cells means no plasma cells and no germinal centers, which explains both the low levels of every immunoglobulin class and the tiny tonsils and nodes. T cells are intact, so most viral infections are controlled, except enteroviruses, which need neutralizing antibody to clear; this is why echovirus meningoencephalitis and live oral polio vaccine are dangerous. The disease is X-linked recessive, so affected patients are nearly always boys.

points: B cells are usually present in normal numbers but fail to become plasma cells.
Low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM; poor response to vaccines.
Onset is often in the 20s to 40s, so a new adult with recurrent pneumonia fits.
Recurrent sinusitis, pneumonia, bronchiectasis, chronic Giardia diarrhea.
Higher risk of autoimmune disease (cytopenias) and lymphoma.
notes.why: In CVID, B cells are present but fail at terminal differentiation and class switching, so few plasma cells form and IgG falls along with IgA, IgM, or both. The cause is heterogeneous, with known genes such as TACI explaining only a minority of cases, which is why the disease usually appears in adulthood and diagnosis rests on low immunoglobulins plus a poor vaccine response. Repeated bacterial lower respiratory infections damage bronchial walls and leave permanent bronchiectasis. The same immune dysregulation that blocks antibody production also allows autoimmune cytopenias and raises the risk of lymphoma.

points: Most common primary immunodeficiency; very low IgA with normal IgG and IgM.
Most people have no symptoms; some get sinus, lung, and Giardia infections.
Linked to celiac disease and other autoimmune diseases.
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis after transfusion of blood products that contain IgA.
IgA-based tests (such as IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase) are falsely negative; use IgG-based celiac tests.
notes.why: Secretory IgM can partly replace IgA at mucosal surfaces, which is why most people with IgA deficiency have no symptoms. Because the patient has never made IgA, the immune system can treat IgA in donor blood products as foreign and form anti-IgA antibodies, so a later transfusion of IgA-containing plasma can trigger anaphylaxis. Any test that measures an IgA antibody, such as IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase, reads falsely negative because the patient cannot make IgA, so the IgG version of the test must be used.

points: 22q11.2 deletion (TBX1 gene); third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail to develop.
No thymus means few T cells: viral and fungal infections.
Absent or small parathyroids mean hypocalcemia: tetany or seizures in the newborn.
Conotruncal heart defects: truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch.
Abnormal facies and cleft palate.
notes.why: The 22q11.2 deletion removes TBX1, a transcription factor needed for normal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and the pharyngeal arch structures that neural crest cells populate. The third pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroids, and the fourth forms the superior parathyroids, so one embryologic defect explains both T cell deficiency and hypocalcemia from low PTH. Neural crest cells also form the aorticopulmonary septum, which explains the conotruncal heart defects. The degree of T cell deficiency depends on how much thymic tissue remains, so most patients have partial rather than complete loss.

points: No working T cells, so B cells also get no help; most common cause is X-linked IL2RG (common gamma chain) mutation.
Other causes: adenosine deaminase deficiency (toxic metabolites kill lymphocytes), RAG1 or RAG2 mutation.
Infant with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, thrush, Pneumocystis pneumonia, severe viral infections.
Absent thymic shadow on chest x-ray; low TRECs on newborn screening.
Live vaccines (rotavirus, BCG, MMR, varicella) can cause fatal infection.
Nonirradiated blood carries donor T cells that cause graft-versus-host disease; give irradiated products.
notes.why: The common gamma chain is shared by the receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21, and IL-7 signaling is required for T cell development, so IL2RG mutations block T and NK cell development; B cells may be present but cannot make useful antibody without T cell help. In ADA deficiency, deoxyadenosine builds up as dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and starves dividing lymphocytes of deoxynucleotides. RAG1 and RAG2 cut DNA for V(D)J recombination, so without them no T or B cell receptors form. TRECs are DNA circles left by T cell receptor rearrangement, so they are low when T cells fail to develop.

tricks.label: CATCH-22
tricks.text: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, from the 22q11.2 deletion in DiGeorge syndrome.

tricks.label: B for Bacteria, T for the rest
tricks.text: Antibody defects mainly let in encapsulated bacteria and enteroviruses. T cell defects let in viruses, fungi, and Pneumocystis. If both groups show up in a baby, think SCID.

tricks.label: Bruton is a baby boy, CVID is a grown-up
tricks.text: XLA shows up in boys after 6 months with no B cells. CVID shows up in adults of either sex with B cells present but no plasma cells.

highYield: Boy over 6 months with recurrent otitis, pneumonia, absent B cells, and no tonsils: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (BTK).
Adult with new recurrent sinusitis, pneumonia, Giardia, low IgG and normal B cell count: CVID.
Anaphylaxis during a first blood transfusion: selective IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies.
Newborn with tetany, truncus arteriosus, and cleft palate: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2).
Infant with thrush, Pneumocystis pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, and no thymic shadow: SCID.
Recurrent Neisseria meningitis: terminal complement deficiency; screen with CH50.
S aureus and Aspergillus abscesses: phagocyte defect; order a DHR test.
pitfalls: XLA has absent B cells; CVID usually has normal B cell numbers. Both have low IgG.
Selective IgA deficiency gives false-negative IgA celiac serology; check total IgA or use IgG-based tests.
DiGeorge and SCID both lack a thymic shadow; DiGeorge adds hypocalcemia, heart defects, and facial changes.
Antibody defects rarely show up before 6 months because maternal IgG still protects the infant.

summary: This unit covers immune deficiency acquired after birth, from medications and from HIV. The exam asks you to link a drug to the infection it unmasks, to trace HIV from entry to AIDS, to read HIV tests, and to predict which opportunistic infection or cancer appears at a given CD4 count.

points: Glucocorticoids: block cytokine gene transcription and cause lymphopenia; risk of Pneumocystis and fungal infection.
Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus): block calcineurin, so NFAT cannot switch on the IL-2 gene and T cells make no IL-2; viral, fungal, and Pneumocystis infections.
TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept): granulomas break down; latent tuberculosis reactivates. Screen for latent TB first.
Rituximab (anti-CD20): depletes B cells; hepatitis B reactivation (and PML from JC virus). Screen for hepatitis B first.
Chemotherapy: neutropenia (ANC below 500 cells per mm3 is severe) leads to gram-negative bacteremia (including Pseudomonas) and Candida or Aspergillus.
notes.why: Each drug removes one specific defense, and the infection that follows is the one that defense normally contains. Glucocorticoids inhibit NF-kappaB and AP-1 driven transcription of cytokines such as IL-1, IL-2, and TNF and redistribute lymphocytes out of the blood, so T cell and macrophage function falls broadly. TNF-alpha keeps macrophages activated and holds granulomas together, so blocking it lets latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis escape. Rituximab removes the B cells that help keep hepatitis B suppressed, and severe neutropenia removes the phagocytes that clear gram-negative bacteria and molds.

points: Enveloped retrovirus (lentivirus) with two copies of positive-sense single-stranded RNA.
gag: p24 capsid (and p17 matrix).
pol: reverse transcriptase (RNA to DNA), integrase (inserts DNA into host genome), protease (cleaves precursor proteins to mature virions).
env: gp160 cut into gp120 (binds CD4 and a coreceptor) and gp41 (fusion).
Coreceptor: CCR5 on macrophages and T cells early; CXCR4 on T cells often later.
CCR5 delta32 homozygotes lack surface CCR5 and resist infection by CCR5-using strains.
notes.why: gp120 binds CD4 and then a chemokine coreceptor, which changes the shape of gp41 so it inserts into the host membrane and fuses the viral envelope with the cell. Reverse transcriptase copies the RNA genome into double-stranded DNA, and integrase inserts this provirus into host DNA, which is why infection is lifelong and why each enzyme is a drug target. Protease must cleave the gag and gag-pol polyproteins for new virions to mature and become infectious. Without CCR5 on the cell surface, CCR5-tropic strains, which dominate transmission, cannot enter.

points: Spread by sex, blood (shared needles, transfusion), and mother to child (birth, breastfeeding).
Acute retroviral syndrome about 2 to 4 weeks after exposure: fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, rash; very high viral load.
Clinical latency: few symptoms for years, but the virus keeps replicating in lymphoid tissue and CD4 counts fall.
AIDS: CD4 below 200 cells per mm3 or any AIDS-defining illness.
notes.why: In acute infection the virus replicates unchecked in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, destroying a large share of mucosal CD4 memory T cells and producing a very high viral load, which makes this the most contagious period. CD8 T cells and antibodies then lower the viral load to a set point, and a higher set point predicts faster progression. During clinical latency, ongoing replication, direct cytopathic killing, and chronic immune activation steadily deplete CD4 T cells. Once the count falls below 200 cells per mm3, cell-mediated immunity can no longer contain opportunistic pathogens.

points: Screen: fourth generation immunoassay detects p24 antigen plus HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, so it turns positive earlier than antibody-only tests.
If positive: HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibody differentiation assay; if that is negative or unclear, HIV-1 RNA (nucleic acid) test.
CD4 count stages immune damage; viral load measures replication and response to therapy.
Infants under 18 months: maternal IgG crosses the placenta, so antibody tests are positive whether or not the baby is infected; use HIV nucleic acid testing.
notes.why: p24 antigen appears in blood before antibodies form, so a combined antigen and antibody test closes the window period sooner than an antibody-only test. The differentiation assay confirms antibody and separates HIV-1 from HIV-2; if it is negative or indeterminate after a reactive screen, the patient may have acute infection with p24 present but antibodies not yet formed, which the RNA test detects. In infants, transplacental maternal IgG can persist up to 18 months, so only direct detection of viral nucleic acid shows true infection.

points: Kaposi sarcoma: HHV-8; purple skin, mouth, gut, or lung lesions of spindle cells and slit-like vessels.
Primary CNS lymphoma: EBV-driven B cell lymphoma; usually one ring-enhancing lesion at CD4 below about 50.
HIV-associated nephropathy: collapsing FSGS with heavy proteinuria, mostly in patients of African ancestry.
HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder and distal symmetric sensory neuropathy.
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome: weeks after starting antiretroviral therapy, recovering T cells attack existing infections, so the patient gets worse.
notes.why: Loss of CD4 T cell help removes the cytotoxic T cell surveillance that normally keeps latent oncogenic herpesviruses in check. HHV-8 drives spindle cells of endothelial origin to proliferate and form leaky slit-like vessels in Kaposi sarcoma, and EBV drives uncontrolled B cell proliferation in primary CNS lymphoma. IRIS shows the opposite problem: antiretroviral therapy restores CD4 T cells, which then mount a strong inflammatory response against antigens of an infection that was already present.

tricks.label: 200, 100, 50 ladder
tricks.text: Pneumocystis below 200. Toxoplasma below 100. CMV retinitis and MAC below 50. Each step down the ladder adds rarer, deeper infections.

tricks.label: One lesion or many
tricks.text: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS point to Toxoplasma. A single ring-enhancing lesion with EBV DNA in the CSF points to primary CNS lymphoma.

tricks.label: Screen before you suppress
tricks.text: Before a TNF inhibitor, check for latent TB. Before rituximab, check for hepatitis B. The drug wakes up whatever is sleeping.

highYield: Positive HIV test in a 4-month-old of an infected mother proves nothing; order nucleic acid testing.
Fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy 3 weeks after exposure with negative antibody test: acute HIV; check RNA or p24.
CCR5 delta32 homozygote resists CCR5-using HIV strains.
Patient on infliximab with fever, cough, and upper lobe cavity: reactivated tuberculosis.
Rising liver enzymes after rituximab: hepatitis B reactivation.
Purple skin plaques in AIDS: Kaposi sarcoma from HHV-8.
Patient worsens weeks after starting antiretroviral therapy: immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
Nephrotic proteinuria in HIV: collapsing FSGS.
pitfalls: Viral load tracks replication; CD4 count tracks immune damage. Do not use one for the job of the other.
Thrush scrapes off; oral hairy leukoplakia does not.
Toxoplasma lesions are usually multiple; CNS lymphoma is usually solitary.
AIDS can be diagnosed with a CD4 above 200 if an AIDS-defining illness is present.

summary: This unit covers the four types of hypersensitivity and the diseases built on each: anaphylaxis, antibody attacks on cells and tissues, immune complex diseases such as lupus, and T cell injury such as granulomas and transplant rejection. The exam asks you to classify a disease by mechanism, then predict its labs, biopsy, and complications.

points: First exposure: Th2 cells release IL-4, B cells switch to IgE, IgE coats mast cells through FcepsilonRI.
Re-exposure: allergen cross-links bound IgE and mast cells degranulate within minutes (histamine, tryptase).
Late phase hours later: leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and eosinophil influx.
Anaphylaxis triggers: peanut and other foods, insect stings, penicillin, latex.
Signs: urticaria, angioedema, wheeze from bronchospasm, hypotension from vasodilation and leaky vessels.
Serum tryptase peaks about 1 to 2 hours after onset and confirms mast cell activation; a normal value does not rule it out.
notes.why: Sensitization sets up the reaction: Th2 cytokines IL-4 and IL-13 drive class switching to IgE, which binds the high-affinity FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils and stays there. On re-exposure, a multivalent allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules and triggers degranulation of preformed histamine and tryptase within minutes. The same signal starts synthesis of leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, and cytokines such as IL-5, which recruit eosinophils and produce the late phase hours later. Histamine and leukotrienes increase vascular permeability and contract bronchial smooth muscle, which explains hypotension, angioedema, and wheeze.

notes.h: Type II: antibody against cells or matrix
points: Warm AIHA: IgG binds red cells at body temperature; splenic macrophages remove membrane, making spherocytes. Causes: idiopathic, SLE, CLL, drugs.
Cold agglutinin disease: IgM binds red cells in cool extremities and fixes complement; acrocyanosis; Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV.
Both have a positive direct Coombs test (IgG in warm, C3 in cold).
Goodpasture: antibodies to the alpha3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes; hemoptysis, rapidly progressive crescentic GN, linear IgG.
Myasthenia gravis: antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor (or MuSK) block and remove receptors; the muscle cell lives but cannot respond.
Myasthenia: fatigable ptosis, diplopia, proximal weakness; thymic hyperplasia common, thymoma in some.
notes.why: In type II reactions, antibody binds antigen fixed on a cell or in a basement membrane and causes damage by opsonization, complement activation, or receptor interference. Warm IgG coats red cells, and splenic macrophages remove pieces of membrane, leaving spherocytes; IgM strongly activates complement, so cold agglutinin disease leaves C3 on red cells. In Goodpasture, antibody to the same collagen in alveolar and glomerular basement membranes fixes complement and recruits neutrophils, giving linear staining. In myasthenia gravis, antibodies block acetylcholine receptors and speed their internalization, so fewer receptors respond to repeated nerve impulses and weakness worsens with use.

points: Antigen and antibody form complexes that lodge in vessels, glomeruli, and joints, fix complement, and draw in neutrophils.
SLE: apoptotic nuclear debris is cleared poorly, so nuclear antigens drive autoantibodies and immune complexes.
SLE labs: ANA (sensitive), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (specific), anti-histone (drug-induced), low C3 and C4 in flares.
SLE features: young woman with malar rash, photosensitivity, nonerosive arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, nephritis with wire loops, Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
Antiphospholipid syndrome: venous and arterial clots and recurrent pregnancy loss.
Polyarteritis nodosa: medium vessels, hepatitis B link, ANCA-negative, spares the lung; fibrinoid necrosis at different stages, renal and mesenteric microaneurysms.
PSGN: 1 to 4 weeks after group A strep throat or skin infection; cola urine, edema, hypertension, low C3, high ASO or anti-DNase B; subepithelial humps, granular immunofluorescence.
RA: HLA-DR4, antibodies to citrullinated peptides; synovial pannus erodes cartilage and bone.
RA: symmetric MCP, PIP, and wrist joints, DIP spared; rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, nodules; Felty syndrome is RA plus splenomegaly plus neutropenia.
Serum sickness: about 1 to 2 weeks after foreign protein; fever, urticaria, arthralgia, proteinuria, low complement. Arthus reaction is the local version at an injection site.
notes.why: Immune complexes cause injury where they deposit, wherever the original antigen came from, which is why one disease can hit skin, joints, kidneys, and serosa together. Complexes trapped in vessel walls and glomeruli activate complement, C5a draws in neutrophils, and their enzymes cause fibrinoid necrosis. Complement consumption explains the low C3 and C4 in SLE flares and serum sickness and the low C3 in PSGN. In RA, citrullinated self-proteins in a susceptible host (HLA-DR4) drive autoreactive T and B cells, and cytokines such as TNF and IL-6 turn synovium into invasive pannus.

points: Th1 cells make IFN-gamma that activates macrophages into epithelioid cells and giant cells; TNF keeps the granuloma intact.
Caseating granulomas with central necrosis: tuberculosis. Noncaseating: sarcoidosis.
Tuberculin skin test: read induration at 48 to 72 hours; a positive test means prior sensitization to mycobacterial antigens.
Sarcoidosis: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, high ACE, hypercalcemia (macrophages make calcitriol), uveitis, erythema nodosum.
Lofgren syndrome: erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar adenopathy, and arthritis; usually resolves.
notes.why: In type IV reactions the injury comes from T cells, which need time to be recruited and activated, so the response peaks 48 to 72 hours after re-exposure. Antigen-presenting cells make IL-12, which pushes CD4 T cells toward Th1, and Th1 IFN-gamma activates macrophages, which become epithelioid cells and fuse into multinucleated giant cells to wall off antigen they cannot clear. In sarcoidosis, activated granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase outside the control of PTH, so calcitriol rises and causes hypercalcemia. The tuberculin test is a small local version of the same memory Th1 response to injected mycobacterial protein.

points: Hyperacute: preformed antibodies (ABO, HLA) in minutes; graft clots and turns dusky.
Acute: weeks to months; host T cells against donor MHC, or donor-specific antibodies.
Chronic: months to years; graft arteriosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis, bronchiolitis obliterans in lung grafts.
Graft-versus-host disease: donor T cells attack host skin (rash), liver (jaundice), and gut (diarrhea).
notes.why: Timing reveals the mechanism. Hyperacute rejection needs preformed antibody, which binds graft endothelium at once, fixes complement, and causes thrombosis within minutes. Acute rejection takes days to weeks because host T cells must recognize donor MHC and expand, and chronic rejection reflects ongoing low-grade immune injury to vessels that thickens the intima and causes ischemic fibrosis. GVHD reverses the direction: immunocompetent donor T cells in a graft such as bone marrow recognize host MHC as foreign and attack the epithelium of skin, liver, and gut.

tricks.label: ACID
tricks.text: Anaphylactic and Atopic (type I), Cytotoxic antibody (type II), Immune complex (type III), Delayed T cell (type IV).

tricks.label: Linear vs lumpy
tricks.text: Linear IgG along the basement membrane means antibody bound to the membrane itself (Goodpasture). Granular, lumpy deposits mean immune complexes that landed there (PSGN, lupus).

tricks.label: Count the joints
tricks.text: RA hits MCP, PIP, and wrists and spares the DIP joints. Osteoarthritis loves the DIP joints. Lupus arthritis looks like RA but does not erode bone.

highYield: Hives, wheeze, and hypotension minutes after a bee sting with high tryptase: type I anaphylaxis.
Young man with hemoptysis, crescentic GN, linear IgG: Goodpasture (alpha3 chain of type IV collagen).
Ptosis that worsens by evening with an anterior mediastinal mass: myasthenia gravis with thymoma.
Child with cola urine 2 weeks after strep throat, low C3: PSGN.
Anti-dsDNA rising with low C3 and C4: active lupus nephritis.
Hepatitis B, ANCA-negative, renal and mesenteric microaneurysms, normal lungs: polyarteritis nodosa.
Hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum, high calcium, noncaseating granulomas: sarcoidosis.
Fever, rash, arthralgia, and low complement 10 days after antithymocyte globulin: serum sickness.
pitfalls: Myasthenia gravis is type II even though cells are not killed; antibody blocks receptor function.
Hyperacute rejection is antibody-mediated (type II); acute cellular rejection is T cell mediated (type IV).
PAN spares the lungs; granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis do not.
TB skin test induration is measured; redness alone is not a positive result.
Rheumatoid factor is common in other diseases; anti-CCP is the more specific RA test.

Heart: Libman-Sacks endocarditis, serositis
Blood: cytopenias; antiphospholipid clots

Re-exposure: allergen cross-links adjacent bound IgE

Antibodies form against streptococcal antigens over 1 to 4 weeks
Immune complexes accumulate in glomeruli as subepithelial humps

summary: This unit covers systemic sclerosis, acute rheumatic fever, Sjogren syndrome, neonatal lupus from anti-Ro antibodies, and mixed connective tissue disease. The exam pairs each with its autoantibody or trigger and asks you to predict the organs it damages and its long-term complications.

points: Starts with injury to small vessel endothelium and autoimmune activation.
T cells and macrophages release TGF-beta, which drives fibroblasts to lay down excess collagen.
Result: thick, tight skin, narrowed small arteries, and fibrosis of internal organs.
Raynaud phenomenon is often the first sign.
Esophageal smooth muscle is replaced by fibrosis: dysmotility, reflux, Barrett risk.
Interstitial lung disease is a leading cause of death; pulmonary hypertension also occurs.
notes.why: Systemic sclerosis joins three processes: small vessel injury, autoimmunity, and fibrosis. Endothelial damage and intimal proliferation narrow small arteries, which explains Raynaud phenomenon, digital ulcers, and later pulmonary arterial hypertension and renal crisis. Activated T cells and macrophages release TGF-beta and other profibrotic signals that turn fibroblasts into myofibroblasts, which lay down collagen in skin, lung interstitium, and the muscular wall of the gut. In the esophagus, fibrosis replaces smooth muscle in the lower two thirds and weakens the lower sphincter, so peristalsis fails and acid refluxes freely.

points: Diffuse: skin thickening reaches the trunk and upper arms; early organ disease; anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I).
Diffuse disease carries the risk of scleroderma renal crisis (sudden severe hypertension and kidney failure).
Limited: skin of fingers, forearms, and face; slower course; anticentromere antibody.
Limited disease shows CREST and late pulmonary arterial hypertension.
notes.why: The two forms differ in how far the skin disease spreads, which autoantibody is present, and which organs are at risk, so the antibody helps predict the course. Anti-topoisomerase I goes with rapid diffuse skin disease and interstitial lung disease, and in renal crisis, narrowed renal arterioles lower renal perfusion and drive renin release, causing severe hypertension and acute kidney injury. Anticentromere goes with limited disease, where gradual obliteration of small pulmonary vessels causes pulmonary arterial hypertension years later.

points: Follows untreated group A strep pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks; skin infection does not cause it.
Molecular mimicry: antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac proteins (type II hypersensitivity).
Pancarditis: endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium are all inflamed.
Aschoff bodies: foci of inflammation with fibrinoid change, lymphocytes, and Anitschkow cells (caterpillar-shaped nuclei).
Diagnosis: evidence of recent strep (ASO, anti-DNase B, culture) plus two major Jones criteria, or one major and two minor.
Years of repeated attacks scar the mitral valve, causing mitral stenosis with fused commissures.
notes.why: Antibodies made against streptococcal M protein cross-react with similar epitopes on cardiac myosin and valve tissue and on basal ganglia neurons, which explains carditis and Sydenham chorea. Only pharyngeal infection triggers this response, which is why impetigo can cause PSGN but not rheumatic fever. Antibodies and cross-reactive T cells inflame all layers of the heart, and as inflamed valves heal they thicken, calcify, and fuse at the commissures. The mitral valve is involved most often, so repeated attacks lead to mitral stenosis.

points: Lymphocytes infiltrate and destroy salivary and lacrimal glands.
Dry mouth (xerostomia) with dental caries and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca); parotid swelling.
Antibodies: anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB); rheumatoid factor is often positive.
Often occurs with RA (secondary Sjogren).
Higher risk of marginal zone (MALT) B cell lymphoma; new or persistent parotid enlargement is a warning sign.
notes.why: CD4 T cells and B cells infiltrate exocrine glands and destroy acinar and ductal tissue, so tear and saliva production falls. Saliva normally buffers acid and washes away bacteria, which is why dry mouth leads to rampant dental caries. Chronic stimulation of B cells inside the glands, the same activity that produces anti-Ro and anti-La, can select a clonal B cell population, which explains the risk of MALT lymphoma.

points: Maternal anti-Ro (SSA) IgG crosses the placenta and injures the fetal AV node.
Result: congenital complete heart block with fetal bradycardia; it is permanent.
Neonatal rash and cytopenias fade over months as maternal IgG is cleared.
The mother may have Sjogren syndrome, SLE, or no symptoms at all.
Mixed connective tissue disease: overlap of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis features.
MCTD marker: high-titer anti-U1 RNP; Raynaud and puffy hands are common.
notes.why: Maternal IgG anti-Ro is actively carried across the placenta by FcRn, binds fetal cardiac tissue, and causes inflammation and fibrosis of the conduction system around the AV node, usually in the second trimester. Scarred conduction tissue does not regenerate, so the heart block persists after maternal antibody is gone. The rash and cytopenias depend on circulating antibody alone, so they clear as maternal IgG is catabolized over about 6 months. In MCTD, high-titer anti-U1 RNP marks a distinct overlap pattern that helps separate it from SLE or systemic sclerosis alone.

rows: Truncal skin thickening, early organ disease
Same, slower and confined to distal skin
Calcinosis, Raynaud, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia
Group A strep pharyngitis; ASO, anti-DNase B
Dry eyes, dry mouth, parotid swelling
Marginal zone lymphoma; neonatal heart block in offspring

charts.title: Jones major criteria
rows: New murmur, pericardial rub, heart failure
Painless nodules over bony surfaces and tendons
Pink rings with clear centers on the trunk

tricks.label: J (heart) NES
tricks.text: Joints (migratory polyarthritis), heart (carditis), Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea. These are the Jones major criteria.

tricks.label: CREST
tricks.text: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia: limited systemic sclerosis with anticentromere antibody.

tricks.label: Ro crosses to the heart
tricks.text: Anti-Ro is IgG, so it crosses the placenta. Rash and low counts fade as the IgG is cleared, but the scarred AV node stays blocked.

highYield: Anti-Scl-70 with truncal skin thickening and lung fibrosis: diffuse systemic sclerosis.
Anticentromere with telangiectasia and later pulmonary hypertension: CREST.
Sudden severe hypertension and rising creatinine in diffuse scleroderma: renal crisis.
Child with migratory arthritis and new murmur 3 weeks after strep throat: acute rheumatic fever.
Anitschkow cells in an Aschoff body: rheumatic carditis.
Mitral stenosis decades after childhood rheumatic fever.
Newborn with complete heart block and a mother with dry eyes: anti-Ro (SSA).
Raynaud, puffy hands, myositis, and high-titer anti-U1 RNP: MCTD.
pitfalls: Strep skin infection can cause PSGN but not rheumatic fever; rheumatic fever needs pharyngitis.
Rheumatic fever is type II (antibody mimicry); PSGN is type III (immune complexes).
Anti-Scl-70 means diffuse disease; anticentromere means limited disease.
In neonatal lupus, heart block is permanent while rash and cytopenias resolve.

About 2 to 4 weeks delay

Mitral stenosis years later

summary: This unit covers amyloidosis, where misfolded proteins pile up outside cells and stiffen organs. The exam asks you to recognize amyloid on a stain, to tell primary (AL) from secondary (AA) amyloid by the protein and the setting, and to match the other amyloid proteins to their diseases.

points: Proteins misfold into beta-pleated sheets that stack into rigid fibrils.
Fibrils are deposited outside cells, crowding tissue and stiffening organs.
H&E: pink, glassy, featureless material.
Congo red stain: apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
Biopsy: abdominal fat pad aspirate is the easy first site; an affected organ (kidney, heart) gives the highest yield.
notes.why: Amyloid is a shared shape that many unrelated proteins can adopt. Misfolded proteins stack into cross-beta-pleated sheet fibrils that resist breakdown by proteases, so they accumulate outside cells, press on parenchymal cells, and stiffen tissue. Congo red dye binds in an ordered way along the regular fibril structure, which produces apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Systemic amyloid often involves small vessels throughout the body, so a fat pad aspirate can find it without biopsy of a vital organ.

points: A monoclonal plasma cell clone makes excess immunoglobulin light chains (lambda more often than kappa).
A plasma cell dyscrasia; some patients also have multiple myeloma.
Find the clone with serum and urine protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, and serum free light chains.
Heart: restrictive cardiomyopathy with thick walls but low-voltage ECG.
Kidney: nephrotic syndrome.
Tongue and skin: macroglossia, periorbital purpura from fragile vessels.
Nerves: carpal tunnel syndrome and peripheral or autonomic neuropathy.
notes.why: AL amyloid comes from a clonal plasma cell population whose free light chains, more often lambda, are prone to misfold. Light chains circulate everywhere, so deposits are systemic and reach heart, kidney, nerves, tongue, and vessel walls. In the myocardium, deposits thicken the walls without true muscle hypertrophy and replace electrically active tissue, so the echocardiogram shows thick walls while the ECG shows low voltage, and the stiff ventricle fills poorly, giving restrictive physiology. Amyloid in vessel walls makes them fragile, which is why minor straining causes periorbital purpura.

points: Serum amyloid A is an acute-phase protein the liver makes under IL-1, IL-6, and TNF.
Years of high SAA lead to AA deposits.
Settings: rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic infections (tuberculosis, osteomyelitis, bronchiectasis).
Familial Mediterranean fever: MEFV (pyrin) mutation, recurrent fever and serositis, AA amyloid if untreated.
Kidney is hit most: proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, kidney failure.
notes.why: Chronic inflammation keeps IL-1, IL-6, and TNF high, and these cytokines make hepatocytes produce serum amyloid A continuously. Incomplete breakdown of SAA leaves an N-terminal fragment that forms AA fibrils. The kidney is the main target, and glomerular deposits disrupt the filtration barrier, causing proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. In familial Mediterranean fever, mutant pyrin allows excess inflammasome activity and IL-1 release, which drives repeated inflammatory attacks and keeps SAA high.

points: Beta2-microglobulin: long-term dialysis; carpal tunnel and joint deposits.
Transthyretin, wild type: older adults, mainly the heart (age-related cardiac amyloid).
Transthyretin, mutant: hereditary cardiomyopathy and neuropathy.
A-beta (from amyloid precursor protein): Alzheimer plaques and vessel walls.
Calcitonin: amyloid in the stroma of medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Amylin (islet amyloid polypeptide): pancreatic islets in type 2 diabetes.
notes.why: Each amyloid protein reflects a setting in which a normal protein is present in excess or becomes unstable. Beta2-microglobulin, the light chain of MHC class I, is normally filtered and catabolized by the kidney and is poorly removed by dialysis, so it builds up in patients on long-term dialysis. Transthyretin normally circulates as a tetramer that carries thyroxine and retinol-binding protein, and a mutation or aging destabilizes the tetramer into monomers that misfold. Secretory cells and tumors, such as C cells making calcitonin and beta cells making amylin, deposit their own products locally.

charts.title: Amyloid proteins and their settings
rows: RA, IBD, chronic infection, familial Mediterranean fever

charts.title: AL vs AA amyloidosis
rows: RA, IBD, TB, familial Mediterranean fever

tricks.label: AL is Light chain, AA is Acute phase
tricks.text: The second letter tells you the protein: AL comes from Light chains of a plasma cell clone. AA comes from serum Amyloid A, an acute-phase protein of chronic inflammation.

tricks.label: Thick heart, small voltage
tricks.text: A thick ventricular wall on echo with low-voltage QRS on ECG means protein deposits are thickening the wall. Think amyloid.

tricks.label: Green under the lens
tricks.text: Congo red alone looks red. The apple-green color appears only under polarized light, and that is the finding that proves amyloid.

highYield: Apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light: amyloid.
Macroglossia, periorbital purpura, and nephrotic syndrome with a monoclonal light chain: AL amyloidosis.
Long-standing RA or Crohn disease with new nephrotic syndrome: AA amyloidosis.
Recurrent fever and serositis in a patient of Mediterranean ancestry, then proteinuria: familial Mediterranean fever with AA amyloid.
Carpal tunnel syndrome after years of dialysis: beta2-microglobulin amyloid.
Older man with heart failure, thick walls, low voltage, and no light chain: wild-type transthyretin.
Amyloid in the stroma of a thyroid tumor: medullary carcinoma (calcitonin).
pitfalls: Amyloid is extracellular; intracellular inclusions (such as tau tangles) are a different finding.
AL amyloid can occur without overt myeloma; a monoclonal light chain is enough.
AA amyloid rarely hits the heart; AL and transthyretin amyloid are the cardiac ones.
Fat pad biopsy can miss amyloid; a negative result does not rule it out.

AA: serum amyloid A, chronic inflammation
Beta2-microglobulin: long-term dialysis

Kidney: nephrotic syndrome
Tongue: macroglossia

Find the clone with electrophoresis and free light chains

steps: Clonal plasma cells proliferate in the bone marrow
Excess free light chains, more often lambda, enter the blood
Light chains misfold into beta-pleated sheet fibrils

Restrictive cardiomyopathy, nephrotic syndrome, neuropathy, and macroglossia

Macrophages release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF
Liver produces serum amyloid A continuously
Incomplete breakdown of SAA leaves fragments that form AA fibrils
AA fibrils deposit, mainly in the kidney

Tetramer dissociates into monomers
Monomers misfold and assemble into amyloid fibrils

Restrictive cardiomyopathy, with neuropathy in hereditary forms

summary: This unit covers the classic childhood and systemic infections: the rash illnesses, Hib, influenza, mumps, EBV and CMV mononucleosis, and toxoplasmosis. The exam gives you a rash pattern, an age, and a timeline, and asks you to name the cause and predict the complication, especially in pregnancy and in weak immune systems.

points: Measles: fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, then Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa, then a rash spreading from the head down.
Measles complications: pneumonia (main cause of death), encephalitis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later; vitamin A deficiency worsens outcomes.
Rubella (enveloped positive-sense RNA virus): mild fever, pink rash spreading from face to trunk, postauricular and occipital lymph nodes, arthralgia in adult women.
Congenital rubella after infection in the first trimester: cataracts, sensorineural deafness, PDA, blueberry muffin rash.
Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19): slapped cheek, then lacy reticular rash on the limbs; adults get symmetric hand and wrist arthropathy.
Parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors: aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease or spherocytosis, hydrops fetalis in pregnancy.
Roseola (HHV-6, less often HHV-7): child under 2 with 3 to 5 days of high fever, often 39 to 40 °C (102.2 to 104 °F), then a truncal rash as the fever breaks; febrile seizures.
Scarlet fever (group A strep toxin): sandpaper rash, circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, Pastia lines, peeling of hands and feet about a week later.
notes.why: Rash timing reflects how each organism spreads and how the immune system responds. Measles spreads from the respiratory tract to lymphoid tissue and then by viremia to skin, the rash appears with the T cell response to infected cells, and the virus suppresses immunity for months afterward, which helps explain secondary bacterial pneumonia. Parvovirus B19 enters erythroid progenitors through the P antigen (globoside) and kills them, pausing red cell production for about a week, which matters when red cell survival is short or demand is high, as in hemolytic anemia or the fetus. Scarlet fever comes from streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins.

points: Type b has a polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule; disease is now mostly in unvaccinated young children.
Epiglottitis: high fever, drooling, muffled voice, inspiratory stridor, child sitting forward.
Other invasive Hib disease: meningitis, bacteremia, pneumonia, septic arthritis.
Nontypeable strains (no capsule) cause mucosal infections: otitis media, sinusitis, conjunctivitis.
notes.why: The polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule resists phagocytosis and complement, so clearing Hib depends on anticapsular antibody that opsonizes it. Children under about 2 years respond poorly to T-independent polysaccharide antigens, which is why invasive disease peaked in this age group before vaccination. The conjugate vaccine links PRP to a protein carrier, recruiting T cell help to produce a strong IgG memory response in infants. Nontypeable strains lack a capsule, so they rarely invade the bloodstream and instead cause local mucosal infections.

points: Abrupt fever, myalgia, headache, dry cough, and malaise.
Primary viral pneumonia: rapid, diffuse infiltrates and hypoxia.
Secondary bacterial pneumonia: patient improves, then worsens; S aureus or S pneumoniae.
Reye syndrome: aspirin given to a child with influenza or varicella causes liver failure (microvesicular fat) and encephalopathy.
notes.why: Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium for entry, and neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release new virions. The virus kills ciliated epithelial cells, stripping the mucociliary barrier and exposing the basement membrane, so bacteria such as S aureus and S pneumoniae can invade during recovery. The abrupt systemic symptoms come from cytokines such as IL-6 and interferons released in response to infection. In Reye syndrome, salicylate injures hepatic mitochondria, causing microvesicular steatosis, hyperammonemia, and cerebral edema.

points: EBV infects B cells through CD21; reactive CD8 T cells appear in blood as atypical lymphocytes.
Adolescent with fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical nodes, and splenomegaly; heterophile (Monospot) positive.
Amoxicillin or ampicillin given for presumed strep throat causes a diffuse rash.
Complications: splenic rupture (avoid contact sports), hepatitis, cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Cancers: Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lymphomas in transplant and AIDS patients.
CMV: heterophile-negative mono, owl's eye intranuclear inclusions in enlarged cells.
Congenital CMV: periventricular calcifications and sensorineural hearing loss.
CMV in transplant and AIDS patients: retinitis, colitis, pneumonitis.
notes.why: EBV gp350 binds CD21 (complement receptor 2) on B cells, and infected B cells proliferate; the atypical lymphocytes in blood are mostly CD8 T cells responding to them. Heterophile antibodies are part of a polyclonal IgM response from activated B cells and happen to agglutinate sheep or horse red cells. EBV stays latent in memory B cells, and its latent proteins drive B cell proliferation and block apoptosis, which explains the B cell lymphomas that appear when T cell surveillance fails. CMV infects many cell types, including fibroblasts, endothelium, and monocytes, so it causes heterophile-negative mono and organ disease in immunosuppressed hosts.

points: Mumps: painful parotid swelling; orchitis in postpubertal males, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis.
Serum amylase rises with parotitis alone; lipase points to pancreatitis.
Toxoplasma gondii: cat feces (oocysts) or undercooked meat (tissue cysts).
Healthy host: often silent or mono-like lymphadenopathy.
Congenital: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcifications.
AIDS with CD4 below 100: multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions.
notes.why: Mumps spreads by viremia to glandular tissue and the meninges, so parotitis, orchitis, pancreatitis, and aseptic meningitis are all parts of one infection. Inflamed parotids release salivary amylase, which raises serum amylase without pancreatic damage, so lipase separates the two. Toxoplasma tachyzoites are controlled by IFN-gamma from T cells and activated macrophages, which forces them into dormant tissue cysts in brain and muscle; when CD4 counts fall below about 100, cysts reactivate and form multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions. A primary infection during pregnancy lets tachyzoites cross the placenta and infect the fetal brain and retina.

tricks.text: Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis come first. Koplik spots follow, then the rash moves from head to toe.

tricks.label: Roseola rash follows the fever
tricks.text: In roseola the rash shows up only after the fever breaks. In measles and scarlet fever the child still has a fever when the rash appears.

tricks.label: Where the calcium lands
tricks.text: Congenital CMV leaves calcium around the ventricles (periventricular). Congenital toxoplasmosis scatters it through the brain (diffuse).

highYield: Child with sickle cell disease, sudden pallor, and very low reticulocyte count: parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis.
Unvaccinated toddler with drooling, stridor, and high fever: Hib epiglottitis.

Postpubertal male with parotid swelling then testicular pain: mumps orchitis.

pitfalls: Heterophile-negative mono is often CMV; young children with EBV can also be heterophile-negative.
Scarlet fever can lead to rheumatic fever and PSGN; strep skin infection leads only to PSGN.
Measles spreads head to toe and the child looks sick; rubella spreads the same way but the child looks well.
In fifth disease, the child is no longer contagious once the rash appears.
High amylase in mumps does not prove pancreatitis; parotitis raises amylase too.
